title: The Busbar Answers
passages:
The busbar answered her open palm immediately. Its reader flared and traced *19* onto the single bright strand left in the wire. The frozen tag vibrated against Voss's spine, found the number, and clicked home. The count finished at Operator 19. The amber leg hissed once and went dark.

Second Adeyemi reached for the tag, but Adeyemi caught her wrist. "No," she said. "You're not finishing this." She pulled the figure's tag free before the sleeping Operators 19 could react. The tag was warm, its ink still wet, naming a return occupant who was already gone.

Voss turned around. "You let go," she said. "Five is unstuck."

Adeyemi held up her palm. Her number was gone, the wire spent, and her hand felt lighter than it had in years. "I signed HOLD wrong. Now it's your turn to decide what Five means."

Behind them, the cracked cradles exhaled. Thirty sleepers sat up straight, eyes on the tag in Adeyemi's hand, waiting for the next signature.

The ink dried faster than wet ink should. It pulled tight on the tag's face, and the smear of a return occupant resolved into letters Adeyemi had not put there. *SENN.* Under it, smaller, the way the station wrote the things it wanted most: *unfiled.*

Senn made a sound like a kettle deciding. "That's my name," they said, and then, because they could not help themselves, "spelled right, which is more than the station manages for anyone else."

The slate on the deck plate reconsidered. *OPERATOR 19 — NUMBER SPENT*, it printed, then scratched the line out with a sound like a nail dragged over tin. *SIGNATURE REQUIRED.* It did not want Adeyemi anymore. It wanted a hand that still had something left to burn.

Thirty hands went up at once.

Every one of them wore 19. Thirty cradles' worth of the same woman, same scar over the same eyebrow, same spent look, and not one number between them the station could tell apart. The slate printed *19* and waited, and printed it again, and the reader on the busbar clicked through all thirty palms and found the same answer thirty times.

"Well," said Voss, still facing the wrong way, still unreadable, still the reason the Figure in the hatch could not close the count. "You've built a lock with thirty identical keys and thrown away the teeth."

"Give me a second," Adeyemi said.

"You don't have a second. You spent it." Voss nodded at the tag. "But *they* do."

Senn was already reaching, mist-hand and solid hand both, and behind them the nearest cracked cradle split with a sound like ice giving way.

Senn caught the tag with the solid hand. The mist hand went through it and came away thinner, vapor threading off toward the hatch. "Signing spends me," they said. "Which half?" Voss didn't turn. "The one you'd rather keep."

Then the cradle split all the way open, and the breath that came out of it was cold enough to fog the deck. It rolled across the thirty sleepers and all of them blinked at once, in sync, like one animal waking. All but the one at the end of the row. She kept her palm flat on the deck plate, and when the busbar reader crossed it, it printed nothing at all. *UNNUMBERED*, said the slate, and rejected her, and rejected 19 again.

"I already signed once," the woman said, without looking up. "Didn't get to keep the receipt."

"That's not an answer," Adeyemi said. "That's a threat with paperwork."

The tag's ink rippled in Senn's fist, still wet, still deciding whose name it wanted. Behind them the hatch sighed open an inch, and the Figure stepped out of it holding a fresh tag, already printing. A stalled count, it turned out, only needed to be started again.

The fresh tag finished printing while the Figure stood in the doorway, and the letters slid out one by one: *END OF ROW — OPERATOR 19 — FIRST SIGNATURE — HOLD*. Adeyemi laughed, but it came out wrong, all the way up in her throat. "You think I want a first signature?" she said. "I spent mine getting a tag with no name."

"Then you should be glad," the woman at the end of the row said, and she was standing now, both hands at her sides, not hiding the palm. "Because I did sign. I signed HOLD. The station read it, filed it wrong, spent the number on me before I could burn it. That's why I'm unnumbered. That's why I never got the receipt." Voss said, very quietly, "Then the copy is the one who spent." It wasn't a question. The Figure answered before Voss could finish. "The copy is what the station made from the breath she didn't spend. The first signature is her. The strike is Five. The count restarts from here."

Senn looked at the fresh tag, then at their own wrist, where the mist was coming off thinner every second. "How much does it cost to take a first signature?" they asked. The Figure's single optic moved to Senn. "The tag takes the hand that signs. The hand takes the number it remembers. You remember with the solid. The solid anchors. The mist forgets. You can hold with the solid and let the mist pay, or hold with the mist and let the solid pay. Which half signs?" Senn's solid hand steadied. Their mist hand drifted like smoke. "The solid signs," they said. "The mist pays. It was always going to pay." They pressed the solid hand to the fresh tag. The mist went through the ink and did not come back. The tag drank the signature and then, because it rewrote as it dried, printed a final line: *Senn — UNFILED — RETURN OCCUPANT: THE FIRST OPERATOR 19*. The room didn't know what to look at. Adeyemi looked at the end-of-row woman. The end-of-row woman looked back with the calm of someone who had been waiting for the station to admit it was wrong.

The slate didn't care about calm. It printed *Five* and kept going, and the fifth cradle's sleeper sat up gasping, eyes wide and wet, and the end-of-row woman didn't move to catch her. Adeyemi did, stepping forward on legs that felt like they belonged to someone else, and caught the woman's shoulders before she could slump back into the cold vent. "Hey," Adeyemi said. "You're Five. You're filed. Breathe."

Five's fingers closed on Adeyemi's wrist, surprisingly strong. "You're thin," she said. "You spent it. You spent the breath to stop at four."

"I stalled it," Adeyemi corrected. "Didn't stop it. Just bought you a minute."

The Figure hadn't moved from the hatch. Its fresh tag still glowed *END OF ROW — OPERATOR 19 — FIRST SIGNATURE — HOLD* in the dim light, and the ink hadn't dried. Senn stood beside them, solid hand pressed to the tag's surface, mist hand gone entirely now — just a faint shimmer at the wrist where it used to be. They looked at Five, then at the end-of-row woman, then at Adeyemi. "The tag names me return occupant for the first Operator 19," they said. "But the first Operator 19 is standing right there. So what am I returning to?"

"Your body," the end-of-row woman said. "The one the station filed in 004. The one that's been breathing for you while you were unfiled." She tilted her head at Voss. "And hers. And the thirty sleepers who just woke up numbered. The station has bodies. It needs occupants. The tag assigns them."

Voss's jaw tightened. "So we sign the tag. Each of us. And the station files us proper."

"The tag takes the hand that signs," the Figure said. "The hand takes the number it remembers. Who remembers what?"

Five let go of Adeyemi's wrist and stood on her own, swaying slightly. She looked at her palm — blank, unnumbered, fresh as the day she was decanted. Then she looked at the end-of-row woman. "I remember you choosing me," Five said. "Before numbers. Before the count. You put your hand on my cradle and said *this one stays*." She smiled, small and sharp. "You didn't sign HOLD for the station. You signed it for me."

The end-of-row woman's smile didn't waver. "I signed it for both of us. The station just filed it wrong."

*Six,* printed the slate. A sixth cradle went dark down the row. *Seven.* Another.

"Count's moving again," Senn said. Their voice was flat. "We need to sign. All of us. Before it files us wrong."

Adeyemi looked at her own hand — the one the slate called spent, the one that held copy-breath thin as vapor. She looked at Voss, who had turned her back on the Figure once already. She looked at Five, who remembered being chosen before she had a number. And she looked at the tag in Senn's solid grip, still wet, still deciding.

"Then we sign," Adeyemi said. "But not the way the station wants."

Adeyemi pressed her palm to the wet tag before the count could lick the next number off the slate. Her copy-breath came up thin and silver, not the dark ink the station expected, but the tag drank it anyway. She dragged her fingers across the gloss in a loop that meant nothing to a machine and everything to her. *Not filed,* she thought. *Not numbered.*

The end-of-row woman stepped up beside her, unnumbered and unrepentant, and pressed her own palm over Adeyemi's. The fresh tag flared, the word *HOLD* burning darker under two unnumbered hands. Five followed, her blank palm landing on top, and Senn's solid grip held the corner down so the ink couldn't curl away. The Figure at the hatch clicked once, a sound like a bone settling, and raised its own empty tag toward them.

The slate stuttered. *Seven* hung in the air, then dropped to *Six*. The count had reversed, breathing back into the dark cradles instead of burning them out. Thirty sleepers remained awake, but the filing hand had nothing left to steer.

Adeyemi didn't lower her hand. "Again," she said. "Every strike."

The Maintenance Figure came forward, and Adeyemi kept her palm on the wet tag. The hatch light caught the fresh tag in its other hand—dry, uninked, breathing no breath at all. Its filing hand lifted, wrist straight, the way a hand raised only by protocol raises a hand. "Strike confirmation requires a numbered hand," it said. "The number is six. Six is spent."

Senn's solid hand tightened on the tag. The end-of-row woman didn't flinch. Five watched the Figure's face, or the place where a face should be. Adeyemi kept her palm pressed to the gloss and did not pull away. "Surrender the solid hand," the Figure said, "or keep it. Protocol does not leave a copy-breath loop open at a spent number."

The Figure's dry tag trembled. The slate under it flickered *Six*, and the sound was like a breath being taken. Adeyemi's copy-breath came up thin, silver, and wrong. The end-of-row woman's peace was a mask; Five's certainty was new and bright and not yet tested. "Keep it," Senn said, and the word cost them. The solid hand stayed on the tag, gripping the wet edge, and the Figure's filing hand stopped just beside it, unable to close the distance without breaking protocol. The Figure clicked once, then withdrew its fresh tag. "Next strike," it said. "You will need another hand."

Adeyemi didn't lower her own. Her copy-breath thinned to nothing. The tag drank what it could. The slate waited at six, and Adeyemi’s hand was already shaking.
